text: Choosing what to remember; inserting by size.

Designing a DP is mostly choosing the state. Ask: (1) what is the last decision? (2) what must I remember about the past to make every future decision? Keep exactly that, nothing more. Then the transition is "try every last decision" and its cost decides whether you need an optimisation (18.2).

Useful moves when a state seems impossible: build the object step by step in a clever order (insert numbers by size, not by position); count something else (its complement, or "at least k" then subtract); add a dimension for the one fact that matters; swap state and answer when the answer is small and a quantity is large (f[value] = smallest cost). 1 2 3 insert 4 at the end: +0 before 3: +1, before 2: +2, at the front: +3 inversions new largest: +1 inversion per number it jumps

Count permutations of 1..n with exactly k inversions (P2513). Building by position needs to remember which numbers are left: too much. Insert the numbers by size instead: putting i into a permutation of 1..i − 1 creates t new inversions, for any t from 0 to i − 1, whatever the order of the others.
So f[i][j] = Σt=0..min(j, i−1) f[i−1][j−t]. That sum is a window of the previous row: keep its prefix sums and every state costs O(1). O(nk) instead of O(n²k).
Check: permutations of 1..4 with one inversion are 2134, 1324, 1243: 3. Of 1..3 with three inversions only 321: 1.
Subtracting prefix sums under a modulus can go negative: add MOD before taking %. When the window is "everything up to j" (lo ≤ 0) no subtraction is needed.
The rows only need the previous row; with n, k ≤ 1000 the full table is fine, but rolling two rows saves memory when it is not.
Prefix sums, monotone queues, slope optimisation.
An optimisation keeps the same states and transitions but computes "min / max / sum over a range of previous states" faster. Look at the shape of that range and that cost.

Little bird (P3572): from tree j the bird flies to any of the next k trees; landing on a tree that is not lower costs 1. f[i] = min over j in [i − k, i − 1] of f[j] + (h[j] ≤ h[i]). The window slides by one each step: a monotone queue.

Only f matters first; among equal f a higher tree is better (it is less likely to cost 1). Keep the queue sorted by (f ascending, h descending): pop from the back anything worse than the new tree, pop from the front anything outside the window.

Why the front is enough: the front has the smallest f, and among those the highest tree. Any other j in the window has f ≥ f[front]; if f is larger by 1 it can at best tie, so it never wins. O(n) per query.
Multiple knapsack, stock trading with a cool-down (P2569) and the waltz on a moving floor (P2254) all have "best over the last k" transitions: the same queue.
never best dashed: slope 2a x = s[j]
Toy boxes (P3195): put toys j+1..i in one box; the cost is (s[i] − s[j] − L′)² with s = prefix length + count and L′ = L + 1.
Expand with a = s[i] − L′, b = s[j]: f[i] = a² + minj (f[j] + b² − 2ab). Each j is a point (b, f[j] + b²); for a given i we want the point that minimises y − 2a·x.

That is a line of slope 2a touching the set of points from below: only the lower convex hull matters. Here x = s[j] and the slope 2a both increase with i, so the hull is a queue: add new points at the back, and drop points from the front once the next one is better.

Compare slopes by cross-multiplying, never by dividing: x strictly increases here (every toy has length ≥ 1), so the signs are safe and there is no rounding. Each index enters and leaves the queue once: O(n).

If the query slopes are not monotone (任务安排 P5785 allows negative times), keep the whole hull and binary-search the touching point: O(log n). If the points do not arrive in x order (货币兑换 P4027), use CDQ divide and conquer or a balanced tree.
The products can reach (5·10⁷)² ≈ 2.5·10¹⁵: long long is required, and the cross-multiplied comparisons may need __int128 when values are larger.
